title: Sunscreen is overwhelmingly promoted on TikTok, but content with misinformation exhibits proportionally high levels of audience interaction
screen_reason: Cross-sectional content analysis of 971 of the most-viewed sunscreen-related TikTok videos, coded by two researchers against an explicit definition of sunscreen misinformation. It reports the share of videos carrying that misinformation at three levels of strictness (58/971 = 6.0% with any health-risk critique; 23/971 = 2.4% with broad critique of sunscreen as such; 16/971 = 1.6% critiquing without any promotion, i.e. categorically dissuading use). These are shares of items classified misleading with a stated denominator - CONTENT.

estimates.country: Not stated; English-caption TikTok videos worldwide (non-English hashtags such as #protectorsolar were excluded and videos with no English caption were dropped). Authors are Canadian
estimates.date: Hashtag identification 26 September and 4 October 2024; scraping and coding thereafter (exact scrape date not reported); manuscript received 2 August 2025
estimates.measure_type: % of the most-viewed sunscreen-related TikTok videos containing sunscreen health-risk misinformation, broad or product-specific (the paper's headline figure)
estimates.value_raw: n = 58, 6.0% of 971 ('Total with health issues and harms (in either broad or specific) 58 (6.0)')
estimates.denominator: 971 of the most-viewed publicly accessible TikTok videos with English captions, drawn from the five most-used sunscreen hashtags (#sunscreen, #sunscreenviral, #spf, #sunscreenreview, #sunprotection), one video per unique account, 2.47 billion views in total
estimates.definition: Video included either broad critique of sunscreen (it causes health harms or prevents the benefits of sun exposure, including that it is unnecessary or ineffective) OR product-specific health-risk concerns about particular sunscreen brands or formulations. Non-health critiques (texture, scent, white cast, greasiness, irritation) were captured separately and are NOT in this numerator.
estimates.misinfo_def: "sunscreen misinformation was defined as when TikTok content critiqued sunscreen for either having harmful effects on one's body or conversely preventing the benefits of sun exposure, which included ideas that sunscreen is unnecessary or ineffective. ... Sunscreen misinformation was thus defined from a public health perspective where TikToks, in one form or another, dissuaded its use to the detriment of its valuable health benefits."
estimates.source_quote:
In total, (n = 58, 6.0%) TikToks included either 
broad or specific concerns around sunscreen health risks.
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Sunscreen critique', p. 7; Table 1, p. 6; Discussion, p. 10
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two coders coded all 971 videos using a coding frame built iteratively (three coders each viewed 100 videos to draft it, then tested it on 50 more each). Quality control: after round one each coder audited 100 of the other's videos, any category showing variability was re-checked across the entire dataset by the original coder, each coder then did a further randomized 100-video check, and all ambiguous cases were jointly coded to consensus. NO inter-coder reliability statistic (kappa or percent agreement) is reported - agreement was produced by consensus rather than measured. The truth standard is the authors' public-health judgement, backed by cited scientific sources stating that no widely used chemical sunscreen ingredient is known to be harmful.
estimates.moderator_quote: We contracted an Apify-hosted data scraper to download a maximum of 1010 of the most viewed publicly accessible TikTok URLs using each of the five hashtags. ... the total sum of 5,040 downloaded TikToks (8.7 billion views) was compiled into one Google Docs spreadsheet and organized based on view count. With the objective of reaching a finalized data set of approximately 1,000 of the most viewed TikToks, we first removed the 3,040 least viewed TikToks from the list, then removed all additional TikToks from the same user account, save for each unique account's most viewed TikTok. ... Next, we removed all TikToks with no English language text in its caption.
estimates.notes: borderline = true on this row only, for one specific reason: 41 of the 58 videos are product-specific health-risk critiques, and the paper itself concedes that "not all sunscreen critique is categorically unjustified" (it cites the 2021 benzene recalls and the Australian CHOICE SPF-labelling tests). A wholly accurate video raising a genuine product concern could therefore land in this numerator, which is exactly the situation the instructions warn about. The construct stays CONTENT rather than QUALITY because the coding is an explicit misinformation classification against a stated public-health truth standard, not an instrument score - but the numerator is permissive, and the two stricter variants extracted alongside it (2.4% and 1.6%) bracket the same corpus without that problem. Denominator is a rank-truncated most-viewed, hashtag-selected, one-video-per-account set on a single health topic, hence denom_scope topical + denom_selection curated; it is emphatically not a census of sunscreen TikToks (the five hashtags alone cover >2.9 million videos).

estimates.country: Not stated; English-caption TikTok videos worldwide
estimates.date: Hashtag identification 26 September and 4 October 2024; scraping and coding thereafter
estimates.measure_type: % of the most-viewed sunscreen-related TikTok videos containing BROAD critique of sunscreen as such - that it causes health harms or prevents the benefits of sun exposure (stricter definition: excludes product-specific critique)
estimates.value_raw: n = 23, 2.4% of 971 (of which prevents health benefits including 'unnecessary' n = 12, 1.2%; causes health harms n = 15, 1.5%)
estimates.denominator: The same 971 most-viewed English-caption sunscreen TikTok videos
estimates.definition: Video critiqued sunscreen broadly - any and all sunscreens as a sun-protection tool - rather than a specific brand or product, on the grounds that it prevents health benefits (including that it is unnecessary; e.g. blocks vitamin D, prevents a beneficial tan, UV damage is overrated) or causes health harms (e.g. endocrine disruptor, carcinogenic, toxic, contains microplastics, taints breastmilk).
estimates.misinfo_def: "sunscreen misinformation was defined as when TikTok content critiqued sunscreen for either having harmful effects on one's body or conversely preventing the benefits of sun exposure, which included ideas that sunscreen is unnecessary or ineffective." An important coding distinction was "capturing and distinguishing between broad sunscreen critique (any and all sunscreens as a sun protection tool) versus critique of specific sunscreen brands or products".
estimates.source_quote: A total of (n = 23, 2.4%) TikToks included broad critique about sunscreen (not product specific) on grounds that it either prevented health benefits (n = 12, 1.2%) or caused health harms (n = 15, 1.5%) (Table 1 and Box 1).
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Sunscreen critique', p. 7; Table 1, p. 6; examples in Box 1, p. 7
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same two-coder consensus procedure as the headline row; no kappa reported. Box 1 lists the exact claim types counted (vitamin D/tanning benefits, 'not necessary to use', sunburns not dangerous, endocrine disruption, carcinogens, microplastics, toxicity, breastmilk, coral reefs, ingestion).
estimates.moderator_quote: An important coding distinction in the finalized coding frame (S4 File) as a result of this process was capturing and distinguishing between broad sunscreen critique (any and all sunscreens as a sun protection tool) versus critique of specific sunscreen brands or products because of their qualities (e.g., a mineral or "natural" sunscreen versus a chemical sunscreen).
estimates.notes: Stricter definition variant of the 6.0% row: it drops the 41 product-specific health-risk videos and keeps only claims about sunscreen as a category, which is what 'sunscreen misinformation' means in the public debate the paper is responding to. Not borderline, because a broad claim that sunscreen is unnecessary or carcinogenic cannot be true on the paper's stated evidence base. REPORTING DISCREPANCY: the body text gives 2.4% while Table 1 prints 'Broad sunscreen critique 23 (2.6)'. 23/971 = 2.37%, so the text's 2.4% is correct and the table's 2.6 is an error; 2.4 is used here (R8-exact from verbatim counts).

estimates.measure_type: % of the most-viewed sunscreen-related TikTok videos that carried health-risk critique WITHOUT any sunscreen promotion, i.e. categorically dissuading sunscreen use (strictest definition)
estimates.value_raw: n = 16, 1.6% of 971 ('Health issues and harms without promotion 16 (1.6)'); the other 42 (4.3%) combined critique with promotion
estimates.denominator: The same 971 most-viewed English-caption sunscreen TikTok videos
estimates.definition: Video detailed health-risk concerns about sunscreen and did NOT also include any promotion of sunscreen's benefits - the subset the authors describe as 'categorically dissuading its use'.
estimates.misinfo_def: As above: content critiquing sunscreen for harmful effects or for preventing the benefits of sun exposure, judged from a public-health perspective as dissuading its use.
estimates.source_quote:
There was a total of (n = 16, 1.6%) TikToks that only detailed health risk 
concerns around sunscreen without also including sunscreen benefits (Table 1).
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Sunscreen critique', p. 7; Table 1, p. 6; Discussion, p. 10
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same two-coder consensus procedure; no kappa reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: Many of these videos with critique, however, also included a promotion of sunscreen's benefits (n = 42, 4.3%). There was a total of (n = 16, 1.6%) TikToks that only detailed health risk concerns around sunscreen without also including sunscreen benefits.
estimates.notes: Strictest definition variant of the 6.0% row: net-dissuasive content only. This is also the group used in the engagement analysis (the 16 'only critique' videos in Table 2). Useful for the review precisely because the same corpus yields 6.0%, 2.4% and 1.6% depending on where the definitional line is drawn - a clean within-study illustration of definitional sensitivity.

missed_or_uncertain: Seen and NOT extracted. (1) The finer critique sub-categories that are components of rows already extracted: prevents health benefits 12 (1.2%), causes health harms 15 (1.5%), specific-product health issues 41 (4.2%), of which 25 (2.6%) attributed risk to chemical sunscreens, and critique with promotion 42 (4.3%). These are nested inside the three rows above and adding them would double-count the same videos; they are recorded in the rows' value_raw and notes instead. (2) Non-health critiques - white cast 54 (5.6%), greasy/oily 27 (2.8%), irritating skin 31 (3.2%), specific sunscreen critique overall 141 (14.5%) - explicitly excluded by the authors from the misinformation definition. (3) Promotion and production characteristics: sunscreen promotion 843 (86.8%), specific product included 662 (68.2%), product promotion 599 (61.7%), damage 169 (17.4%), acne 149 (15.3%), aging 112 (11.5%), cancer 59 (6.1%), application advice 260 (26.8%), other sun protection 72 (7.4%), purchase options 112 (11.5%), plus the gender and ethnicity of creators - none of these is a misinformation share. (4) Debunking content 28 (2.9%) and debunk responses 13 (1.3%) - corrective content, not misinformation. (5) NO CONCENTRATION ROW IS POSSIBLE, though the paper is about disproportionate engagement: Table 2 gives MEAN views, likes, shares and comments per group (only-critique n = 16: mean views 3,290,496, likes 193,746, shares 13,794, comments 2,211) but never the critique videos' SHARE of total engagement. Multiplying means by counts to get, say, 16 x 13,794 = 220,704 of 3,353,930 total shares would be a computed cross-category sum, which R8 forbids, so R1's requirement for both conc_group_pct and conc_share_pct cannot be met from the printed numbers. An adjudicator wanting a concentration estimate would have to go to the public OSF data (https://osf.io/a594r/). (6) REPORTING DISCREPANCIES worth logging: Table 1 prints 'Broad sunscreen critique 23 (2.6)' where the text says 2.4% (23/971 = 2.4%, text correct); the text says specific-product health-risk videos were '(n = 41, 2.6%)' where Table 1 says 4.2 (41/971 = 4.2%, table correct); Table 1 says 'Female 737 (75.9)' where the text says 'n = 738, 76.0%'; Table 1 says health professionals 'Mentioned in TikToks 15 (1.5)' where the text says 'n = 15, 1.3%'. None of these affects the three extracted values, whose counts and percentages all reproduce exactly.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis of publicly available TikTok data (no ethics review required; AoIR 2019 guidelines followed; data public at https://osf.io/a594r/). Hashtag identification on 26 September 2024, repeated 4 October 2024: 41 sunscreen-related hashtags found, 18 sunscreen-specific ones used in more than 3.8 million TikToks, and the five most used (#sunscreen, #sunscreenviral, #spf, #sunscreenreview, #sunprotection, together >2.9 million TikToks and 76% of posts with sunscreen hashtags) selected. An Apify scraper downloaded up to 1,010 of the most-viewed public URLs per hashtag (5,040 videos, 8.7 billion views); the 3,040 least-viewed were removed, then all but each account's single most-viewed video, then all videos without an English caption, leaving 1,126 URLs; 155 proved inaccessible or non-English during coding, giving the final N = 971 (2.47 billion views, 94.9 million likes, 3.35 million shares, 728,000 comments). Coding frame developed iteratively (three coders x 100 videos, then tested on 50 each); every video coded by two coders, with a 100-video reciprocal audit, whole-dataset re-checks of any variable category showing disagreement, a further randomized 100-video check each, and consensus adjudication of ambiguous cases - but no kappa or percent agreement reported. Engagement compared with Kruskal-Wallis and Dunn's post hoc tests with Bonferroni adjustment in STATA v18.0. Acknowledged limits: no thematic analysis to saturation, no analysis of comments, no per-product SPF verification, English captions only, most-viewed content only, demographic coding by visual interpretation.
rob.item6_quote: For this context, sunscreen misinformation was defined as when TikTok content critiqued sunscreen for either having harmful effects on one's body or conversely preventing the benefits of sun exposure, which included ideas that sunscreen is unnecessary or ineffective. Additional sunscreen critique (e.g., related to texture or scent) was also captured but not categorized as sunscreen health misinformation.
